facts.founded: Created in 2004 from the old Lai Châu province

sections.title: Geography
sections.text: Điện Biên is in the far north-west, bordering Laos and China. At its heart is the Mường Thanh valley, the largest in the north-western mountains. It is about 20 km long and covered in rice fields, and the Nậm Rốm River runs through it.

sections.title: History
sections.text: In the 18th century the rebel leader Hoàng Công Chất made the Mường Thanh valley his base. In 1953–1954 the French built a fortified camp here and were besieged and defeated by the Việt Minh. The battle ended French rule in Indochina and led to the Geneva Accords.

sections.title: Culture
sections.text: The Thái people, both Black and White Thái, have farmed the valley for centuries. Their xòe dance, performed in a circle with linked hands, was listed by UNESCO in 2021. In March the hills turn white with ban (bauhinia) flowers, a symbol of the region in Thái love songs.

etiquette: Keep your voice low at war memorials and cemeteries.
Dress modestly at the museum and monuments.
Join in if you are invited into a xòe circle.

timeline.text: The rebel leader Hoàng Công Chất makes the Mường Thanh valley his base.
French paratroopers land at Điện Biên Phủ and build a fortified camp.
After 56 days of siege, the French garrison surrenders on 7 May.
Điện Biên province is created, and a Victory Monument rises for the 50th anniversary.
The Sơn La dam fills, and its reservoir floods much of the old town of Mường Lay.
A new museum opens for the 60th anniversary of the victory.
UNESCO lists the xòe dance of the Thái people.
Rice fields fill the valley where the battle was fought.
